blocks.text: The eighth people was born at the foot of a mountain range that did have seasons: a brief summer, an autumn the colour of copper, a winter that asked no permission. The clone, remembering Lía, the white strand of hair, Vicente coming to his end in his own time, didn't close the door to wear for them. He left them the cultivated body and the chip, and he also left them the possibility of growing old. He told them on the first day, standing in the first snow, which didn't chill him in the same way, because his young flesh was no longer heading toward an end.

blocks.text: “You can choose not to come to an end,” he said. “I don't, and neither does the man on the shore, and sometimes that's wearying, and sometimes it's a stroke of luck. There's a planet I've seen where they never end and have grown bored of themselves. There's a woman, at a plot, who chose winter so she could keep asking questions. I'm not choosing winter for you. I'm leaving the door open. If you go through it, I won't close it behind you afterwards out of pity.”

blocks.text: Andrés received the letter at nightfall, with Lía having supper in the kitchen, her white strand visible under the lamp, and Iago beside her, who would also come to an end and didn't ask to be spared that fortune. What arrived was, years after the sowing (the bridge sometimes joined times together), a people already entering its first ageing: grey hair, a new slowness, a lower laugh, a recent grave on a hillside, with a date, not polished away.

blocks.text: From the Earth they kept winter, dates, the right to come to an end, the pain of saying goodbye. They forgot, on the other hand, or almost, the stars. They didn't raise their faces. The sky, for them, was what had covered the founder when he left, and looking at it was a way of asking him to come back, or of asking for the eternity they had refused. They preferred the mountains, the copper of autumn, the work of chopping firewood. A child, who hadn't yet been asked whether he wanted to come to an end, pointed one night at a bright spot, and his mother gently lowered his hand.

blocks.text: “That isn't from here,” she said. “Here is the fire, and the soup, and your grandfather, who's gone now.”

blocks.text: The clone, who had come back in passing, the way you come back to a house that isn't quite your own, saw it and didn't correct it straight away. He sat with the old people (truly old, at last, in a people of his) and heard them ask, not for a remedy, but about Lía.

blocks.text: “The one at the plot, the one who comes to an end, is she still keeping to it?” asked a woman with a bent back, with the dignity of a straw hat, though there was no hat. “Does she regret it? Because we do, at times. And at times we don't. We wanted to know whether winter, on Earth, is still a choice or has already become a burden.”

blocks.text: When Andrés received that, he looked at his daughter. He translated it for her, word for word, and Lía didn't answer with a heroine's speech. She sat for a while with the bread in her hand.

blocks.text: “Tell them I don't regret it, not every day,” she said. “Tell them there are mornings when I envy your not coming to an end, Father, and afternoons when I don't envy it at all. Tell them winter isn't a virtue: it's a way of keeping the question from closing. And that if one day they change their minds, I won't call them traitors. I'd only ask them not to call the time they've already lived a flaw.”

blocks.text: That time, the bridge carried the answer. The woman with the bent back heard it, or the clone told her, and she nodded, and asked for the words to be written down for her on paper, not in a chip, so that the paper would wear out too.

blocks.text: Before leaving, the one who searches climbed a height with a child, at night, and named two or three stars for him, without pomp, the way you name a rope and a knot.

blocks.text: “It isn't an altar,” he said. “It's a ceiling. Your mother is right: the fire belongs here. So does the ceiling, if you want to raise your eyes to it. There's no need to ask anyone to come back.”

blocks.text: The child said nothing. He raised his face for a while, and then went back down toward the soup. In that people, it was a tiny and good fissure: not everyone would forget the sky.

blocks.text: When the letter closed, Andrés's eyes were wet and Aya was holding his hand.

blocks.text: “There's a grave with a date,” he said. “In a people I didn't found and that comes out of my memory, someone has truly come to an end. I, here, won't have that date. Vicente had it. Lía will have it. Sometimes I think they got it more right than I did.”

blocks.text: Lía shook her head, gently.
blocks.html: Lía shook her head, gently.

blocks.text: “There isn't a single right answer,” she said. “You stayed so as not to leave Mother on a different shore. I come to an end so I can ask you questions. They've chosen, and at times they regret it, which is proof that they're alive. Don't turn their grave into a lesson against your own house.”

blocks.text: Aya, who didn't grow old as they did, added, with an honesty that came as much from Eva as from herself:
blocks.html: Aya, who didn't grow old as they did, added, with an honesty that came as much from Eva as from herself:

blocks.text: “I won't have that hillside. I'll have this door, and your old age that doesn't come, and Lía's, which will. That isn't entirely fair. Nor is it a flaw a tomato could put right. It's what this family has been able to give of itself.”

blocks.text: In the chip, Eva asked:
blocks.html: In the chip, Eva asked:

blocks.text: *If a people chooses to come to an end and at times regrets it, has the choice failed, or is regret part of winter? And if a child raises his face to a star, does he betray his own people, or widen their ceiling?*

blocks.text: MAY, without judgment:
blocks.html: MAY, without judgment:

blocks.text: *There is a people growing old at the foot of a mountain range. There is a grave with a date. They have asked about Lía. A child has looked at the sky. The founder has left again. That is the fact.*

blocks.text: That night, Lía stayed to sleep in the house, not in the room by the plot. She didn't announce it as a gesture. She lay down in the small bed from when they came back from the Moon, which still, just about, fitted her, and Andrés, passing by, saw the white strand on the pillow and didn't touch it to correct it. It suddenly seemed to him the most exact sign that this shore was still a shore: something, here, was still leaving, and something, here, was still staying, and the two together made up a time that was not eternal and, for that very reason, was enough to love.
